title: Jargon as a Badge of Membership
text:
Every specialised field develops a vocabulary that marks its members and excludes outsiders. A surgeon speaks of an 'anastomosis' where a layperson would say a join, and a lawyer refers to 'consideration' in a sense far removed from ordinary generosity. Such terms allow practitioners to communicate with economy and precision, yet they also create a barrier that can make expertise look like privilege.

Mastering this jargon is therefore less a matter of memorisation than of learning to think within a discipline's assumptions. A newcomer who knows the terms but not the reasoning behind them may sound fluent while still misunderstanding what the words actually commit a speaker to. Genuine command appears when a practitioner can explain a term plainly without distorting its meaning.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what does a surgeon call a join that a layperson would simply describe as a join?
According to the second paragraph, what can a newcomer who knows the terms but not the reasoning behind them appear to be?
options: Fluent, while still misunderstanding the words
Unable to use any technical vocabulary

questions.text: What does the passage imply about the function of jargon?
options: It exists only to confuse outsiders
It enables precision but can also create barriers
It has no purpose beyond decoration
It is always easier than everyday language

questions.text: What does genuine command of jargon look like, according to the passage?
options: Using only the most complicated terms
Explaining a term plainly without distorting its meaning
Refusing to define any term for others
Memorising a long list of words

vocabulary.definition: specialised vocabulary used by a particular profession or group
a surgical joining of two tubular structures, such as blood vessels
something of value exchanged between parties to create a binding agreement
advanced skill and knowledge in a particular field

paragraph_translations: Cada campo especializado desarrolla un vocabulario que marca a sus miembros y excluye a los ajenos. Un cirujano habla de una «anastomosis» donde un profano diría simplemente una unión, y un abogado se refiere a la «contraprestación» en un sentido muy alejado de la generosidad cotidiana. Estos términos permiten a los profesionales comunicarse con economía y precisión, pero también crean una barrera que puede hacer que la pericia parezca privilegio.

Dominar esta jerga es, por tanto, menos una cuestión de memorización que de aprender a pensar dentro de los supuestos de una disciplina. Un recién llegado que conoce los términos pero no el razonamiento que los sostiene puede sonar fluido y, aun así, malinterpretar lo que las palabras comprometen a quien las usa. El dominio genuino aparece cuando el profesional puede explicar un término con claridad sin distorsionar su significado.
